newsitem.title: UK: PRESS DIGEST - Financial Times - Dec 10.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - Financial Times - Dec 10.

text.p: Prepared for Reuters by The Broadcast Monitoring Company
-- CHIRAC AND KOHL CALL ON EU TO FIGHT TERRORISM

A summit between President Jacques Chirac and chancellor Helmut Kohl has failed to resolve Franco-German differences over the implementation of any post-EMU stability pact. Germany is keen to see such a pact, designed to prevent EMU participants breaching deficit targets, applied rigidly, with those in default having large financial penalties applied. France is considerably less keen on political influence being taken away from the application of such rules. Both countries did, however, agree that the EU should pay more attention to combating international crime and terrorism.
-- BASS BID FOR CARLSBERG TO GO TO MMC

A 200 million stg bid by brewers Bass for Carlsberg-Tetley is being referred to the Monopolies & mergers Commission by the Department of Trade and Industry. The DTI announced the decision, noting that it was concerned about the competitive impact of the concentration of production that would arise as a result of a deal that would give Bass a 38 per cent share of the British market. Bass expressed disappointment with the news, though observers in the City expect the company to satisfy competition requirements.
-- EUROTUNNEL TRAFFIC FALLS MORE THAN 40 PER CENT

The recent fire in the Channel Tunnel caused traffic levels for the month of November to decline 40 per cent, according to figures announced on Monday. The number of passengers carried fell to 295,161 for the period. This number was, however, an increase on the volumes carried in November of the preceding year. Traffic levels for lorries for the month also fell 45 percent. Meanwhile, the passenger service Eurostar has announced that since re-starting services, demand for tickets has been steadily improving.
-- FINANCIAL MARKETS REBOUND AFTER SCARE FROM GREENSPAN

A degree of calm returned to world markets on Monday in the wake of turbulence on Friday caused by comments from the chairman of the U.S. Federal Reserve, Alan Greenspan, which were interpreted as an indication that he believed U.S. equities to be overvalued. The comments had also prompted concerns that there would be an increase in U.S. interest rate levels. Meanwhile, three U.K. companies have postponed plans for London stock market launches of shares in the wake of Friday's slump.
-- BANK STAFF URGED TO SUPPORT STRIKE OVER CHRISTMAS HOURS

The banking union Bifu is calling on 35,000 members with the main high street banks to take part in a half-day strike on Christmas Eve. The call comes in the wake of a decision by the banks to remain open for the afternoon, rather than taking the traditional half-day. Two of the main four, Midland and Barclays, have already agreed terms with staff for working the additional time. The union objects to the decision, noting that bank staff deserve time with their families, adding that there is no evidence that there is customer demand for the additional opening.
-- BRUSSELS SPELLS OUT VISION FOR AUDITING

Plans have been detailed by the European Commission for the creation of a single market in statutory corporate auditing. Rather than opting to achieve this goal through legislation, the EU is favouring the fostering of close cooperation with the accountancy profession and hopes to secure the creation of a code of practice to guarantee the independence of auditing practices. The decision not to take the legislative route has been welcomed by the U.K.'s Institute of Chartered Accountants.
-- EU DOUBTS ON BA-AMERICAN ALLIANCE PLAN

A source within the EU has indicated that the commission continues to harbour grave doubts about the competitive impact of plans for a transatlantic alliance between British Airways and American Airlines. The EU is reported to be concerned that recent U.K. indications that the deal might be approved by local regulators if certain landing slots at Heathrow are given up will fail to offset the wider effect on competition of the deal. The U.S., meanwhile, is taking a tougher line on the deal, linking it to the achievement with Britain of an open skies agreement.
-- SWISS BANK SET ASIDE 5 MILLION DOLLARS FOR CIVIL CLAIMS

There are reports that Cantrade, a unit of Union Bank of Switzerland based in the Channel Islands, has set five million dollars aside to deal with claims for compensation that might arise from legal action being taken by investors in relation to losses incurred through the bank by an independent currency trader. Those involved claim the bank should have warned them as was its responsibility given that their investments had a 10 percent downside limit. An out-of-court settlement may be offered.
-- BT MAY BE GIVEN MORE FLEXIBILITY ON PRICES

Oftel on Monday published proposals that could result in British Telecom being given additional freedom in the area of wholesale pricing. Under the plans some 60 per cent of the company's interconnection revenues would be removed from the control of the regulator. Oftel's director-general, Don Cruickshank, has noted that establishing the correct balance in relation to interconnection fees forms a critical element of the overall competitive framework for the industry.
